section.title: The Fall of Tyre
section.sectionRationale: Tyre gloated that Jerusalem's fall would fill her own harbors with the trade Jerusalem once controlled. This oracle answers that greed with a sentence: the LORD Himself will raise up many nations against Tyre, scrape her down to bare rock, and bring her to the Pit, showing that no maritime empire lies outside His sovereign reach.
section.thesis: The LORD who judged Jerusalem for her sin now judges Tyre for gloating over that very judgment and grasping at Jerusalem's ruin for profit, proving that His justice reaches every proud city, however secure it feels behind its walls and its wealth.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Tyre's gloating and the LORD's sentence against her; the specific coming of Nebuchadnezzar's siege; the lament of the princes of the sea over her fall; and Tyre brought down to the Pit among the peoples of old.

units.label: Tyre's gloating and the LORD's sentence

verses.text: In the eleventh month of the twelfth year, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, because Tyre has said of Jerusalem, 'Aha! The gate to the nations is broken; it has swung open to me; now that she lies in ruins I will be filled,'
therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: 'Behold, O Tyre, I am against you, and I will raise up many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves.
They will destroy the walls of Tyre and demolish her towers. I will scrape the soil from her and make her a {{sela|bare rock}}.
She will become a place to spread nets in the sea, for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD. She will become plunder for the nations,
and the villages on her mainland will be slain by the sword. Then they will know that I am the LORD.'

units.label: Nebuchadnezzar's siege declared
units.note: king of kings sent against her

verses.text: For this is what the Lord GOD says: 'Behold, I will bring against Tyre from the north Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, king of kings, with horses and chariots, with cavalry and a great company of troops.
He will slaughter the villages of your mainland with the sword; he will set up siege works against you, build a ramp to your walls, and raise his shields against you.
He will direct the blows of his battering rams against your walls and tear down your towers with his axes.
His multitude of horses will cover you in their dust. When he enters your gates as an army entering a breached city, your walls will shake from the noise of cavalry, wagons, and chariots.
The hooves of his horses will trample all your streets. He will slaughter your people with the sword, and your mighty pillars will fall to the ground.
They will plunder your wealth and pillage your merchandise. They will demolish your walls, tear down your beautiful homes, and throw your stones and timber and soil into the water.
So I will silence the sound of your songs, and the music of your lyres will no longer be heard.
I will make you a bare rock, and you will become a place to spread the fishing nets. You will never be rebuilt, for I, the LORD, have spoken, declares the Lord GOD.'

units.label: The princes of the sea lament

verses.text: This is what the Lord GOD says to Tyre: 'Will not the coastlands quake at the sound of your downfall, when the wounded groan at the slaughter in your midst?

All the princes of the sea will descend from their thrones, remove their robes, and strip off their embroidered garments. Clothed with terror, they will sit on the ground, trembling every moment, appalled over you.

Then they will {{qinah|lament}} for you, saying, 'How you have perished, O city of renown inhabited by seafaring men, she who was powerful on the sea, along with her people, who imposed terror on all peoples!
Now the coastlands tremble on the day of your downfall; the islands in the sea are dismayed by your demise.'
For this is what the Lord GOD says: 'When I make you a desolate city like other deserted cities, and when I raise up the deep against you so that the mighty waters cover you,

then I will bring you down with those who descend to the {{bor|Pit}}, to the people of antiquity. I will make you dwell in the earth below like the ancient ruins, with those who descend to the Pit, so that you will no longer be inhabited or set in splendor in the land of the living.
I will make you an object of horror, and you will be no more. You will be sought, but will never be found,' declares the Lord GOD.”

sela.gloss: A rock or cliff, here stripped bare of soil, buildings, and life. The image is of Tyre's proud, fortified island scraped down to nothing, later fulfilled with striking literalness when Alexander the Great used the rubble of Tyre's abandoned mainland city to build a causeway to her island, scraping the mainland site bare.

qinah.gloss: A funeral dirge or lament, the same form used to mourn a death. The princes of the sea sing a qinah over Tyre as though for a person who has died, underscoring how total and personal her fall would feel to the nations who once depended on her.

bor.gloss: The Pit, a term for the grave or the realm of the dead, often used alongside Sheol. Tyre's descent to the Pit places her among the peoples of antiquity long since dead, a picture of total, final humbling before the living God.

basic.context: Tyre, the great Phoenician sea power built on a fortified island just off the Lebanese coast, responded to Jerusalem's fall with cold satisfaction, expecting to inherit the trade that once flowed through Jerusalem's gate. This oracle answers that greed directly: the LORD will raise up many nations against Tyre, beginning with Nebuchadnezzar, and bring the proud sea city down to a bare rock and finally to the Pit.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes a real, historically anchored judgment fulfilled in two distinct stages: Nebuchadnezzar's actual thirteen year siege of Tyre's mainland settlement, described in verses 7 to 11, and a later, more total devastation of the island fortress itself, fulfilled when Alexander the Great built a causeway from the rubble of the abandoned mainland city in 332 BC, literally scraping the site into the sea as verse 12 describes. The chapter is not a general template for judging cities but a specific, dated prophecy against one real city's specific sin.
basic.originalLanguages: Tyre is reduced to a sela, a bare rock, her proud fortifications and soil scraped away. The princes of the sea raise a qinah, a funeral dirge, over her as though mourning a death, not merely a military defeat. And she is finally brought down to the bor, the Pit, joining the peoples of antiquity in the realm of the dead, a picture of total and final humbling.
basic.typology: Tyre's descent to the Pit, the realm of the dead, foreshadows the biblical pattern of every proud human power eventually humbled before God, a pattern Christ Himself entered and reversed, descending into death yet rising in victory over it, so that all who are His need not fear the Pit's final word.
basic.christ: Tyre's proud self-sufficiency, 'I will be filled' at another's expense, is judged by the God who alone raises up and brings down nations; centuries later, Jesus ministered with grace near Tyre and Sidon, extending faith honoring mercy to a woman from that very region, Matthew 15:21-28, and the early church later found believers already gathered in Tyre, Acts 21:3-6, a living picture of grace reaching the very city once condemned here.
basic.god: God is sovereign over empires and armies alike, raising up 'many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves' and naming Nebuchadnezzar as His own instrument, 'king of kings', language elsewhere reserved for God's ultimate authority. Yet He is also patient with pride's slow discovery of its own smallness, letting the princes of the sea themselves sing the dirge that proves His word true.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 23 gives an earlier, companion oracle against Tyre focused on her trade and her eventual restored profit being set apart to the LORD. Amos 1:9-10 and Joel 3:4-8 condemn Tyre for trading captured Israelites into slavery. Matthew 15:21-28 shows Jesus extending grace to a woman from Tyre and Sidon's region. Revelation 18 echoes this chapter's maritime merchant imagery in describing Babylon's own commercial fall.
basic.oneStory: Tyre's proud, self-serving gloating over Jerusalem's fall is met by the LORD's sovereign hand, working even through pagan Babylon and later Alexander to bring the sea's own princes low. This anticipates the whole biblical pattern that every proud human power is eventually humbled before God, and that even a city as hostile as Tyre is not beyond the reach of the grace that later gathered disciples within her own walls.

context.literary:
Chapter 26 opens the longest block of nation oracles in Ezekiel, the Tyre cycle of chapters 26 to 28, and it is the only one in the cycle given a date, Ezekiel 26:1. The chapter is built from four speeches, and each begins with its own announcement formula, 'this is what the Lord GOD says', in verses 3, 7, 15 and 19. Together they trace a descent. First comes the accusation and a general sentence, then a close-up of the siege, then the world reacting, and last the dive below the earth. The movement is from a city standing proudly to a city that cannot be found.

The sea is the controlling image. Tyre sat in the sea, and the sentence speaks in the language of the sea: 'as the sea brings up its waves', verse 3, the city as a place where nets are spread, verses 5 and 14, the princes of the sea, verse 16, and finally the deep rising over her, verse 19. The sea that made Tyre rich becomes the instrument of her sentence. Her whole identity is turned against her.

The chapter also has a rhythm of verbs. In verses 3 to 6 the LORD speaks in the first person, 'I will raise up', 'I will make', 'I have spoken'. In verses 7 to 11 He names the agent, 'he' shall do these things, and the verbs pile up: slaughter, set up, direct, trample. Then in verse 12 the subject changes to 'they', and the sentence returns to the first person in verses 13 and 14. The change from 'he' to 'they' matters, because it keeps the sweep of the oracle larger than one king.

Another device is the repeated sound of silence. The songs and lyres are silenced in verse 13, the city is 'no more', verse 21, and she is sought but 'never found'. The opening taunt, 'now that she lies in ruins I will be filled', is answered by the closing statement that she will be nowhere. Finally the 'you' addressed in the second person at the end is the language of a funeral, which prepares the lament of chapter 27.
context.historical:
Tyre was the greatest Phoenician port. It sat on a rocky island a short distance off the coast with a settlement on the mainland shore, and the mainland towns and villages supplied it with food, water and timber. That double structure explains the oracle. The 'villages on her mainland', verses 6 and 8, are struck first, and the island fortress later. Acts 12:20 shows the old dependence still operating centuries afterward, for the people of Tyre and Sidon relied on the king's country for food.

The date in verse 1 comes soon after the fall of Jerusalem. The BSB follows what it calls the likely original reading, 'the twelfth year', over the Hebrew text's 'eleventh year', and the twelfth year of the exile is also the year the fugitive arrives, Ezekiel 33:21. Whichever reading is followed, the oracle belongs to the weeks and months right after the city fell, when Tyre was counting her gains.

Her complaint in verse 2 is a trade rival's cheer. Jerusalem commanded overland routes, and 'the gate to the nations' is a merchant's phrase for a competitor's checkpoint now broken open. Tyre had a long history with Israel: Hiram supplied cedar and cypress to David and Solomon for the temple, 1 Kings 5:8-10, in return for food. The alliance had once worked in Israel's favour. Later prophets accuse Tyre of selling captive Judeans, Joel 3:4 to 6, and of breaking a 'covenant of brotherhood', Amos 1:9.

Nebuchadnezzar did attack Tyre. Josephus, citing Phoenician records, says he besieged it for thirteen years, though that comes from a later source and cannot be checked against the text of Ezekiel. Ezekiel himself later says the army worked hard, 'every head was made bald and every shoulder made raw', and got no wages, Ezekiel 29:18. The island held. The fuller devastation came when Alexander the Great, in 332 BC, besieged the island for about seven months and built a causeway from the mainland ruins, which joined the island to the coast.
context.canonical:
Tyre is a recurring figure across the prophets, and Ezekiel 26 sits at the centre of the pattern. Isaiah 23 is a 'burden against Tyre' with the same sea imagery, wailing ships of Tarshish, and Tyre as 'the merchant of the nations', Isaiah 23:1 to 3. Amos 1:9 to 10 and Joel 3:4 to 8 give the accusation of slave trading, and Zechariah 9:3 to 4 returns to the picture of Tyre heaping up silver like dust, only to see the LORD 'cast her wealth into the sea'.

Ezekiel's own book carries the story on. Chapter 27 is a lament over Tyre as a ship, and chapter 28 turns to Tyre's ruler and to Sidon. Chapter 29:17 to 20 supplies a surprising postscript, dated some fifteen years later: the Babylonian army laboured at Tyre without reward, and the LORD gives Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar instead as his wages. The prophet is willing to report that the first stage did not give Babylon what it hoped for.

The New Testament remembers Tyre and Sidon with unexpected tenderness. Jesus says that if the miracles done in Chorazin and Bethsaida had been done in Tyre and Sidon, those cities 'would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes', Matthew 11:21 to 22. He enters the region of Tyre and heals a Gentile woman's daughter, Mark 7:24 to 30. Crowds from Tyre and Sidon come to hear Him, Luke 6:17. Paul stays a week with disciples in Tyre on his last journey, Acts 21:3 to 6.

Isaiah 23:17 to 18 even looks past the judgment, saying that after seventy years the LORD will restore Tyre and her profits will be 'set apart to the LORD'. Psalm 87:4 pictures Tyre among those of whom the LORD says, 'This one was born in Zion.' And the fall of the great merchant city lives on in Revelation 18, where the kings, merchants and sailors lament over Babylon in language that deliberately echoes Ezekiel 26 and 27.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel's first hearers were exiles by the river Chebar, and the word to them was both a comfort and a correction. The comfort is plain. Jerusalem has fallen, and a rival has smiled. The oracle tells them that the rival's smile is noticed and will be wiped off.

The correction is subtler. The exiles were tempted to measure the LORD's power by what they could see. Tyre had walls on the sea, a fleet, and allies, and no army had taken her. Ezekiel tells them that Tyre's security is not security. The One who raised up Babylon against Jerusalem can raise up many nations against Tyre, as the sea brings up its waves. The LORD is not weaker than Tyre's sea walls.

Moses and the prophets taught that no people may profit from another's grief. Tyre's sin is not only gloating but calculation: she looks at a broken city and sees a market. The prophet means his hearers to see that the greed of trade can be as hostile to God's people as the sword.

Finally, Ezekiel wants them to see that the sentence has a purpose. The refrain of verse 6, 'they will know that I am the LORD', tells the exiles that history is being steered toward the recognition of the LORD by every nation.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a specific judgment on a specific city for a specific attitude. It does not teach that commercial cities or trade itself are cursed. Trade is not the sin; Hiram's cedar helped build the temple. The offence is the way Tyre read Jerusalem's catastrophe, as a profit opportunity.

It would be a mistake to treat the details of the siege as a template for how God will treat any rich nation today, or to read every modern harbour city's fortunes as divine comment. Scripture elsewhere warns against such reading: Jesus says that those killed by a falling tower in Siloam were not worse offenders than others, Luke 13:4 to 5.

What carries forward is the principle behind the oracle. We are not to profit from another's ruin, and we are not to put our ultimate security in walls, wealth or position. Proverbs 11:28 says, 'He who trusts in his riches will fall.' The chapter also reminds believers that no commercial or political power is too large for God to humble, which steadies those who live under such powers.

debates.question: Does the prophecy that Tyre would 'never be rebuilt' and be 'no more' fail, since settlements at the site of Tyre continued to exist after Ezekiel's time?

views.label: A prophecy fulfilled in two distinct historical stages
views.case: Verses 7 to 11 describe Nebuchadnezzar's specific siege of Tyre's mainland city, which he did indeed conquer after roughly thirteen years, while verses 3 to 6 and 12 to 14, many nations, scraping the soil into the sea, describe a further, later devastation, fulfilled when Alexander the Great used the rubble of that same abandoned mainland city to build a causeway and finally raze the long unconquered island fortress in 332 BC, an extraordinary, multi-stage fulfillment matching the oracle's specific details.

views.label: The absolute language reflects standard ancient conquest idiom, not a claim about every future settlement
views.case: Ancient Near Eastern royal and prophetic oracles regularly used sweeping language, 'never rebuilt', 'will be no more', to describe decisive, humbling military defeat rather than a literal claim that no settlement would ever again exist at that location; the oracle's central point, Tyre's proud maritime empire being shattered, was thoroughly fulfilled even though a much lesser town later occupied part of the site.

debates.bearing: Both readings affirm that the oracle's central claim, God's sovereign judgment shattering Tyre's pride and imperial power through pagan armies, was fulfilled with real force. The New Testament itself knows a Tyre with disciples in it, Acts 21:3 to 6, so the sentence was never a ban on any future life there.

debates.question: Did Nebuchadnezzar's siege fulfil Ezekiel 26:7 to 14, given that Ezekiel 29:17 to 20 says his army received no wages from Tyre?

views.label: The prophet corrects or completes his own oracle
views.case: Ezekiel 29:18 says the army laboured hard and got nothing from Tyre, so the harsh details of 26:8 to 12 were not fully carried out by Babylon. The LORD then gives Egypt as compensation. On this view prophecy is flexible: the oracle announced the sort of thing God would do, and the prophet reported honestly where Babylon fell short and what remained to be done by others.

views.label: The oracle moves from one agent to many
views.case: In verses 7 to 11 the subject is 'he', Nebuchadnezzar, whose attack is on the mainland villages and the walls. From verse 12 the subject becomes 'they', and verse 3 already spoke of 'many nations'. The oracle never says Nebuchadnezzar will carry off everything. His part is the first wave, and the rest is carried by later hands, so there is no contradiction.

debates.bearing: The text itself, by placing chapter 29's postscript in the same book, shows that Ezekiel was not embarrassed by the question. Either way the lesson holds, that the LORD directs the nations and is not bound to the plans of the kings He uses.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word of the oracle is the taunt in verse 2, and the key verb is 'I will be filled', from the Hebrew root mala. It is a word of appetite: now that Jerusalem is empty, Tyre will be full. The root is worth following into the next two chapters, because Ezekiel returns to it with irony. In 27:25 Tyre is 'filled with heavy cargo in the heart of the sea', and in 28:16 the ruler is 'filled with violence'. The city that hoped to be filled from another's ruin is filled in the end with her own cargo and her own sin. The shape of the three verses reads like a quiet argument.

The Hebrew phrase behind 'I am against you' in verse 3 is a stock formula of confrontation. The LORD speaks it against Jerusalem, Ezekiel 5:8, and later against Sidon, Ezekiel 28:22, and Pharaoh, Ezekiel 29:3. It is a declaration of opposition, a legal and military announcement in one. It tells the reader at the outset that Tyre's sin has been taken personally by God.

The 'bare rock' of verses 4 and 14 is sela, the ordinary word for a cliff or crag, with the added idea of bareness, as when the soil is scraped away to the stone. Tyre's own Hebrew name, Tsor, is closely tied to the word for rock, tsur, and the sentence plays on that. The city that was proud of her rock is told she will be a bare one. Verses 5 and 14 add the fishermen's detail, 'a place to spread nets', which later becomes a different picture in Ezekiel 47:10, where fishermen spread nets along the river of life from En-gedi to En-eglaim. The same image, restored, ends the book.

In verse 17 the 'lament', qinah, is a funeral song. It is the form David used for Saul and Jonathan, 2 Samuel 1:17 to 27, and Ezekiel uses it for the princes of Israel, Ezekiel 19:1, for Tyre, for its ruler in 28:12, and for Pharaoh, Ezekiel 32:2. Its occurrence in verse 17 means the sentence is already being sung as though it were done. The song is placed on the lips of the 'princes of the sea', so that Tyre's own trading partners deliver the eulogy.

Finally, the 'Pit' of verses 20 and 21 is bor. It is the grave, the place of the dead beneath the earth, and it is paired with the 'deep' of verse 19. The word for the deep is tehom, the same word as the primeval deep of Genesis 1:2, and in Jonah's prayer 'the watery depths' close around the drowning man, Jonah 2:5. The Hebrew builds a vertical descent: the sea rises, the deep covers her, she goes down to the Pit. In verse 20 'the land of the living' is where Tyre will no longer be 'set in splendor', and Ezekiel 32:23 uses the same phrase of those who once spread terror there and now lie in the Pit.

typology.type: The proud city brought to the Pit, Ezekiel 26:19-21
typology.fulfillment: Tyre goes down to the Pit among the ancient dead. The pattern of a power humbled by descent is taken up in Christ in a startling reversal. He too goes down into death, Matthew 12:40 and Ephesians 4:9, but not as a sentence for pride. He enters it voluntarily and breaks its power, so that the grave is no longer the last word, Hebrews 2:14-15. Tyre's descent is final: 'you will be sought, but will never be found'. Christ's is temporary, and the tomb is found empty. The correspondence is that He goes where Tyre went, and the escalation is that He returns.

typology.type: The city of the sea cast down, Ezekiel 26:3-5 and 19
typology.fulfillment: The sea city is overwhelmed by waves. A second sea picture stands in the gospels, where a violent windstorm threatens to swamp the disciples' boat and Jesus rebukes the wind and sea, Mark 4:37-41. Tyre's sea turned on her at the LORD's word; the sea obeys Christ's word and the boat is saved. The type is that the same Lord commands the same waters. The fulfilment is that the One whose word could raise the deep over Tyre uses the same word to bring His people through the storm. The pattern is not exact, since Tyre's storm was judgment and the disciples' was a test.

typology.type: Tyre's wealth cast into the sea, and Babylon's fall, Ezekiel 26:12 and Revelation 18
typology.fulfillment: The loot, merchandise and fine houses of Tyre are thrown into the water. Revelation 18 takes this picture and extends it to the whole world system. A mighty angel casts a millstone into the sea and says Babylon will be 'cast down, never to be seen again', Revelation 18:21, and the sound of music is silenced, 18:22, as in Ezekiel 26:13. Mourners stand at a distance, and shipmasters and sailors weep. The type is that every commercial empire that exalts itself over God's people meets the same end. It falls short as a prediction of Tyre specifically, for Revelation's Babylon is larger than any one city.

typology.type: Fishermen's nets on the bare rock, Ezekiel 26:5 and 14
typology.fulfillment: Spreading nets is the sign of a place given over to fishing. In Ezekiel 47:10 it becomes the sign of a place healed, as fishermen line the river that flows from the temple. In the gospels Jesus calls fishermen to become 'fishers of men', Matthew 4:19, and the nets of ruin become nets of mission. The correspondence is real but gentle: the former image of defeat reappears as an image of life. It is a pattern of reuse, not a prediction.

study.christ:
The oracle leads to Christ most clearly through three connections, pride and humility, the sea and the Lord, and Tyre and the gospel itself.

First, pride and humility. The Tyre of Ezekiel 26 says, 'I will be filled', as she stares at another city's ruin. Christ takes the opposite course. 'Though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor, so that through His poverty you might become rich', 2 Corinthians 8:9. Tyre grows rich by another's loss, and Christ gives His own riches to make others rich. Philippians 2:6 to 8 puts it plainly: He did not grasp, He emptied Himself. Tyre's greed is the exact opposite of the logic of the cross.

Second, Christ is the one who rules the sea. The prophet announces that the LORD will raise up the deep against Tyre, verse 19. When the disciples are about to drown in a violent storm, Jesus 'rebuked the wind and the sea' and 'it was perfectly calm', Mark 4:39. The disciples ask 'Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?', Mark 4:41. In the Old Testament, the LORD alone controls the waters, Psalm 89:9. The Gospel claims that Jesus does what only the LORD does, and Ezekiel 26 is one of the places that sets the stage for that claim.

Third, Tyre itself meets Christ. In Matthew 11:21 to 22 Jesus says that Tyre and Sidon would have repented if they had seen what Chorazin saw, and that it will be more bearable for them on the day of judgment. In Mark 7:24 to 30 He goes into the region of Tyre and answers a Gentile woman's faith. The same region the oracle condemned receives mercy at the Lord's hand. Acts 21:3 to 6 shows a church in Tyre. The oracle of judgment does not cancel the gospel; the gospel comes to the very place that was judged.

A caution: Ezekiel 26 does not mention the Messiah, and the sea, the nets and the rock are not coded portraits of Jesus. The link is made by the Bible's own use of the same themes: the sea obeys the LORD, the proud are humbled, the Gentile cities are gathered, and Christ is the one in whom all these themes meet. Where Tyre sought to be filled by taking, He fills by giving, John 1:16.
study.god:
The oracle shows a God who is sovereign over the nations and over nature. He says, 'I will raise up many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves.' The nations are waves and He commands them. Nebuchadnezzar, 'king of kings' in verse 7, is the title his own world used, but Daniel 2:37 says that the God of heaven gave him that sovereignty, and Jeremiah 27:6 calls him 'My servant'. Even the mightiest earthly ruler is on a leash. The oracle teaches the doctrine of providence at the level of history: wars, sieges and trade routes are inside His purposes.

He is personal. The formula 'I am against you' is not an abstract doctrine of justice but a statement of personal opposition. Tyre's cheer at Jerusalem's fall was heard, and it was taken as against Him. This is the God who is known through covenant, who identifies Himself with a ruined city of His people, and who counts a smile at their suffering as a smile at His own.

He is just in a way that fits the offence. Tyre sought to be filled by another's loss; her wealth is plundered, her houses thrown into the sea. She had trusted her walls and the sea; the walls are broken and the sea is the instrument of her ruin. The punishment matches the shape of the sin.

He is true to His word. 'For I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD', verses 5 and 14. That phrase appears like a seal, a statement that what He says will happen. This is the same God who told Ezekiel that when the fugitive arrived his mouth would open, and it did.

He is patient with a purpose. The recognition formula, 'then they will know that I am the LORD', verse 6, shows that He aims at being known, not just at destroying. Even Tyre may know Him, and later Scripture shows that some in Tyre did.

For worship, this chapter invites us to trust God with the kingdoms of the world. It teaches the church not to envy the proud city, Psalm 73:3 and 17, and not to be afraid of her power. We can take hope from the fact that all that humans build in the heart of the sea is held by hands that are not ours, and that the God who silences the songs of the proud is also the God who will fill the mouths of His people with a new song, Revelation 5:9.

crossReferences.note: An earlier burden against Tyre, using the same sea picture. The ships of Tarshish wail, and Tyre is called 'the merchant of the nations'. Reading the two together shows that Ezekiel is not inventing a new charge but standing in a prophetic tradition that saw Tyre's commerce as the heart of her pride.

Looks past the judgment. After seventy years the LORD restores Tyre, and her profits are 'set apart to the LORD'. It helps readers see that the oracle of Ezekiel 26 is not the final word on Tyre, and it matches the later picture of Tyre receiving mercy in the Gospels.

Tyre 'has heaped up silver like dust' and will see the LORD 'cast her wealth into the sea'. It confirms Ezekiel 26:12 from another prophet, with the same destination for Tyre's wealth, the water that was her home.

Dated years later, it reports that Nebuchadnezzar's army laboured at Tyre with no wages, so the LORD gives Egypt instead. It is the prophet's own commentary on the fulfilment of chapter 26, and it shows how the oracle unfolded in more than one stage.

Tyre, Sidon and Philistia are accused of taking the LORD's silver and gold and selling the people of Judah and Jerusalem to the Greeks. It gives specific moral content to the judgment of Ezekiel 26, so that Tyre is not punished only for gloating but for profiting from the traffic in people.

Tyre delivered up a whole congregation of exiles to Edom and broke a covenant of brotherhood, and the LORD sends fire on her walls. The older prophecy names the covenant betrayal behind Ezekiel's 'I am against you', since Tyre and Israel had once been allies.

Hiram of Tyre sends cedar and cypress to Solomon in exchange for food. It shows the friendly side of Tyre's relationship with Israel, and the fact that the city's wealth first served God's house. Her fall in Ezekiel is therefore not an attack on commerce as such but on a particular posture toward God's people.

A mighty angel casts a millstone into the sea, and Babylon is 'never to be seen again' while the music is silenced. The imagery of a sea city sunk and its songs stopped draws directly on Ezekiel 26:13 and 21 and gives the oracle its final, universal form.

Jesus says Tyre and Sidon would have repented in sackcloth and ashes if they had seen His miracles, and that it will be more bearable for them in judgment than for the cities that did see. The condemned city of Ezekiel 26 becomes a standard of what a hearing heart looks like.

The One whom the wind and sea obey is Jesus. Ezekiel 26:3 and 19 show the LORD commanding the waves, and in Mark the disciples ask who this is. The answer the gospel gives is that He does what the LORD does.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a God who separates the waters, and the sea in Scripture is both a gift and a menace. In Genesis 1:2 the deep is the formless water over which the Spirit hovers, and in the flood, Genesis 7:11, the deep breaks open. Ezekiel 26 draws on that memory. When the LORD says He will 'raise up the deep' against Tyre, He is using creation's oldest picture of chaos as the instrument of judgment.

Tyre herself is part of a larger story about the nations and trade. After Babel, the peoples were scattered, Genesis 11. Tyre becomes the great meeting place of those scattered peoples, and Ezekiel 27 will show her trade linking nearly all of them. A city that gathers the nations by commerce is a rival picture to the one that God promised to Abraham, that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3. Tyre is a Babel on the water: unity by wealth and power, apart from God.

The oracle also answers a question from the middle of the story. When Israel fell, did the nations' gods win? Tyre believed she had profited. The LORD says her profit is a mirage, and the sequence of Nebuchadnezzar and then Alexander shows that He moves empires.

Yet the story is not simply condemnation. Tyre appears among the nations of Psalm 87:4, and Isaiah 23:17 to 18 says her wealth will be set apart for the LORD. When Jesus comes to Tyre's region, He receives faith there, Mark 7:24 to 30, and the early church meets in Tyre, Acts 21:3 to 6.

The story ends in Revelation, where the fallen merchant city becomes Babylon and the sea of chaos is no more, Revelation 21:1. In that new creation the nations bring their glory into the city of God, Revelation 21:24, and the ships of Tarshish that once carried Tyre's wealth are pictured in Isaiah 60:9 bringing sons and silver 'to the honor of the LORD your God'. What Tyre used for pride is redeemed for worship.

quiz.q: Why did the LORD pronounce judgment on Tyre in this chapter?

options.text: Because Tyre gloated over Jerusalem's fall, expecting to profit from the trade her ruin left behind.
options.note: Verse 2 gives Tyre's exact words of gloating self interest as the provoking sin.

options.text: Because Tyre had worshiped idols for centuries.
options.note: Idolatry is not the specific accusation named in this chapter; the stated sin is gloating profiteering over Jerusalem's fall.

options.text: Because Tyre had refused to pay tribute to Egypt.
options.note: Not mentioned in this text at all; the accusation concerns her attitude toward Jerusalem's ruin.

options.text: Because Tyre had broken a trade treaty with Israel generations earlier.
options.note: No treaty violation is cited; the specific sin named is her cold, self interested reaction to Jerusalem's fall.

quiz.q: Who does the LORD specifically name as His instrument to bring against Tyre?

options.text: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, called 'king of kings' in this oracle.
options.note: Verse 7 names Nebuchadnezzar directly and gives him this striking title.

options.text: Pharaoh king of Egypt.
options.note: Egypt is not named as the instrument against Tyre in this chapter; that role belongs to Nebuchadnezzar.

options.text: The king of Assyria.
options.note: Assyria had already fallen by this period; the named instrument here is Babylon's king.

options.text: An unnamed coalition of Phoenician rivals.
options.note: The text is specific: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon is named directly as the LORD's chosen instrument.

quiz.q: How do the princes of the sea respond to Tyre's downfall, according to verses 15 to 18?

options.text: They descend from their thrones in terror and raise a funeral lament over her as over the dead.
options.note: Verses 16 to 17 describe exactly this response, trembling and a formal qinah, or lament, for Tyre.

options.text: They celebrate, since Tyre was their commercial rival.
options.note: The text describes mourning and terror, not celebration, among the neighboring princes.

options.text: They immediately send military aid to rebuild Tyre.
options.note: No rescue or rebuilding effort is described; their response is lament and dread, not aid.

options.text: They remain indifferent, unaffected by her fall.
options.note: The text describes strong emotional and physical reactions, trembling, appalled, not indifference.

quiz.q: What does 'bringing Tyre down to the Pit' in verses 19 to 20 picture?

options.text: A total and final humbling, joining Tyre with the long dead peoples of antiquity in the realm of the dead.
options.note: Verse 20 explicitly places Tyre among 'the people of antiquity' who have already descended to the Pit.

options.text: A temporary exile from which Tyre would quickly return to power.
options.note: The imagery describes a final, total humbling, not a brief or reversible exile.

options.text: A literal underground prison built by Babylon for Tyre's leaders.
options.note: The Pit here is a term for the realm of the dead or the grave, not a literal Babylonian prison structure.

options.text: A description only of Tyre's economic decline, with no reference to death or destruction.
options.note: The imagery is explicitly about descent among the dead, a far more total picture than mere economic downturn.

quiz.q: How does history relate to this oracle's specific details about Tyre's destruction?

options.text: Nebuchadnezzar besieged the mainland city for years, and Alexander the Great later used its rubble to build a causeway that finally razed the island fortress, matching the oracle in two stages.
options.note: This two stage historical fulfillment, Babylon then Alexander, is well attested and matches the oracle's specific details, including scraping soil into the sea, verse 12.

options.text: No historical event ever matched any detail of this prophecy.
options.note: Historical sources describe both Nebuchadnezzar's siege and Alexander's causeway built from the old city's rubble, closely matching this oracle.

options.text: Tyre was destroyed in a single, immediate conquest by Nebuchadnezzar alone.
options.note: Nebuchadnezzar's siege did not fully subdue the island fortress; that fell later, to Alexander the Great.

options.text: The prophecy was fulfilled only in a purely symbolic, non historical sense.
options.note: The fulfillment is unusually concrete and historical, not merely symbolic, matching real, datable military events.

questions: Tyre said 'Aha' when Jerusalem fell, hoping to profit from another's ruin. Where have you caught yourself feeling satisfaction, even quietly, at someone else's downfall or misfortune?
Tyre trusted in her island fortress and her wealth to keep her safe from any threat. What fortress, financial, relational, or reputational, are you tempted to trust in more than you trust God?

The LORD calls pagan Nebuchadnezzar His own instrument, 'king of kings,' even though Nebuchadnezzar did not know or serve Him. Where do you see God using circumstances or people outside your control to accomplish His purposes in your life right now?
The princes of the sea mourned Tyre as though for a death, finally seeing what they had refused to see while she stood. What warning are you tempted to ignore until it is too late to act on it?

Grace later reached the very city and region this oracle condemns, in Jesus' ministry near Tyre and Sidon and in the disciples Paul later found there. Who or what feels too far gone or too hostile for God's grace to reach, and how might this chapter's ending in Acts challenge that assumption?

translationNotes.note: The title 'king of kings' applied to Nebuchadnezzar is a striking use of royal language elsewhere associated with supreme authority, underscoring how completely the LORD commands even the greatest pagan rulers as His own instruments.
